rv.q: We’re always entertained, frequently laughing — at the same time, as in certain Wes Anderson movies, there’s something in the extra-stylish surface that keeps deeper feelings at bay.
Cold War Choir Practice helps us laugh to keep from crying, though it might also draw a tear–and make us think about the nature of power.
This spirit of trust and integrity to the world of the play makes Cold War Choir Practice soar.

Reddick’s story delivers so much dizzying suspense (after you’ve figured out what’s going on) that even a huge bomb explosion – Masha Tsimring’s lighting and Kathy Ruvuna’s sound effects make you jump — is something of a letdown.
Reddick's writing retains a sense of play, allowing humor and absurdity to coexist with the darker implications of the story.

This is a surprise and a disappointment, because so much of “Cold War Choir Practice” is so good, not least its first-rate cast led by Alana Raquel Bowers, an adult who is completely convincing as ten-year-old Meek.

So much of what busily precedes and follows this as Meek ruminates, brothers Smooch and Clay confront each other, Puddin complains and accuses, and Virgie’s frame of mind devolves doesn’t seem to make cohesive sense.
But it is a fun, antic, and ingenious show that well deserves this remounting, especially in an increasingly dangerous era when cold war fears almost seem quaint.
Nothing cold about this red-hot show that is not to be missed.
Director Knud Adams proves, once again, his deft ability to sculpt wildly dense material, assembling a first-rate acting company that knows exactly what world they're living in.

The cheeky attitude and comedic timing of Cold War Choir Practice made a scathing criticism of a world on the brink of nuclear war highly entertaining without removing the serious questions about what we laugh at and why.
But the performances and the play’s wonderfully off-kilter imagination make Cold War Choir Practice well worth experiencing.
Reddick has written a play about a working-class Black family navigating impossible choices in 1987, and that play is vital and urgent.
That's not to say that there aren't things to enjoy in Reddick's play... Or that there aren't similar pleasures to be found in the supple staging by Knud Adams.

cn.t: Reddick's genre-bending Cold War comedy earns mostly positive reviews for its imaginative blend of 1980s nostalgia, absurdist humor, and family drama, though some critics find it overly cute or tonally uneven as it shifts from light comedy to darker spy thriller territory.

vr.q: This play couldn't be more relevant and I cannot recommend it enough.
